name: ToMA
main_result: SDXL-base 1024x1024 (ImageNet class prompts): FID 28.88 / DINO 0.068 at 11.0 s/img on V100 (baseline 25.27 at 14.5 s/img), merge ratio 0.5 (about 24% faster); Flux.1-dev 23.4% faster at ratio 0.75 on RTX6000
notes: Tokens are latent tokens inside the transformer blocks of SDXL and Flux. Destination tokens are chosen by greedy facility-location (submodular) maximization over cosine similarity, within local tiles; all tokens are merged into them with an attention-like soft weight matrix, the reduced set passes self-attention, cross-attention and MLP, and the transpose of the merge matrix unmerges back to N tokens. Destinations are reused for 10 denoising steps and merge weights for 5 steps. Latency is the median wall-clock time over 100 runs on RTX6000, V100 and RTX8000; batch size not stated.
evidence: "we propose Token Merge with Attention (ToMA), a training-free framework that bridges this gap by rethinking token merge for GPU-aligned operation" (Sec. 1); "ToMA uses our GPU-optimized facility location algorithm to select a diverse and representative set of “destination” tokens" (Sec. 1); "Merge is then formulated as an attention-like linear transformation for efficient aggregation of non-destination tokens, with unmerge implemented via its inverse transformation" (Sec. 1); "We reuse the destination for 10 denoising steps and reuse merge weights for 5 steps" (Sec. 5.1)

name: SDTM
backbones: SD3 Medium; SD3.5 Large; SD3.5 Large Turbo (MMDiT)
main_result: SD3 Medium 1024x1024 COCO2017 (50-step RF): FID 29.60 / CLIP 0.3224 at 7.07 s, 1.51x (baseline 29.02 / 0.3267 at 10.67 s); SDTM* (adaptive threshold) FID 28.97 at 6.90 s, 1.55x
notes: Two stages over denoising steps. Structure stage (first 40% of steps): windows with high mean cosine similarity (plus a priority for tokens not merged recently) are averaged into one token before MHSA and MLP. Detail stage: tokens with low received attention (inattentiveness from the attention map) are merged into their most similar attentive token before the MLP only. Merged tokens are restored by similarity-based copy blended with the previous step's features. Schedule: the default SDTM uses a hand-set cosine decay of the merge ratio over steps (same for every image); SDTM* uses a per-layer and per-step threshold from a calibration batch, so the count varies per image. Also reweights prompt tokens using categories from ChatGPT. Latency averaged over 5000 COCO images on A100 40G; batch size not stated.
evidence: "Served in a post-training way, the proposed method can be integrated seamlessly into any DiT architecture." (Abstract); "we compute the average cosine similarity within each window w as the similarity priority score" (Sec. 4.1.1); "Utilizing the attention map, which effectively quantifies the relationships between tokens, we identify the inattentive tokens." (Sec. 4.1.2); "This method offers a straightforward approach for dynamically adjusting the merging ratio." (Sec. 4.1.3); "Image generation is a feature-intensive task that necessitates the complete feature map." (Sec. 4.1.4)

name: ToCa
main_result: PixArt-alpha (20 DPM++ steps) COCO2017: FID-30k 28.33 at 5.78 TFLOPs, 1.93x by FLOPs, 0.390 s (baseline 28.09 at 11.18 TFLOPs, 0.682 s), N = 3, R = 70%; OpenSora 2.36x at VBench 78.34 (baseline 79.13)
notes: Feature caching, not sequence shortening: in steps between full computations (every N steps), R% of the tokens in each cross-attention and MLP layer skip computation and reuse their cached output from an earlier step, while all tokens stay in the sequence, so halt is the closest operation. Self-attention layers are fully cached. Caching score from self-attention influence on other tokens and cross-attention entropy (attention statistics) plus cache frequency and a spatial-uniformity rule. Cache ratio is hand-set per layer depth and type (same for every input). Speed-up in Table 1 is by FLOPs; latency on A800 80GB, batch size not stated.
evidence: "we introduce token-wise feature caching, allowing us to adaptively select the most suitable tokens for caching, and further enable us to apply different caching ratios to neural layers in different types and depths" (Abstract); "In the following timesteps, we can skip the computation of some unimportant tokens by re-using their value in the cache C." (Sec. 3.4); "We firstly pre-define the cache ratio R of tokens in each layer" (Sec. 3.4); "estimated with an attention score in self-attention" (Sec. 3.5); "with no requirements for training" (Abstract)

name: DiffCR
backbones: PixArt-Sigma (T2I); Lazy Diffusion (PixArt-alpha based inpainting DiT)
main_result: PixArt-Sigma 512x512 T2I (LAION-5B, 10K images): FID 10.68 / CLIP 0.238 at 13957 GFLOPs, 179.71 s per batch of 16 on A100 (fine-tuned PixArt-Sigma 11.93 / 0.242 at 17362 GFLOPs, 225.38 s), DiffCR-LT, ratio 20%
notes: Mixture-of-depths routing for DiTs: a linear+sigmoid router per layer scores tokens, the top-k pass the whole layer (attention and MLP) and the rest skip it and are concatenated back unchanged (halt). The keep ratio of each layer and of each timestep region is a learned scalar (differentiable via two neighboring 10% bins, MSE loss to a target ratio); at inference the nearest bin is used, same for every image. Inpainting models are fully fine-tuned; the T2I model is fine-tuned with a rank-32 LoRA plus routers. Latency on A100 with batch sizes 16 and 128. The paper links a project page (https://www.haoranyou.com/diffcr), no code URL in the text.
evidence: "each DiT layer includes a router that is fine-tuned jointly with model weights to predict token importance scores" (Abstract); "After passing through the routers, we select the top-k most important tokens for this layer’s processing, while the activations of other tokens are cached and concatenated with the layer outputs, bypassing the entire layer computation, including both attention and MLPs." (Sec. 3.2); "we simply select the nearest bin as the final compression ratio during inference, eliminating any overhead" (Sec. 3.3); "For the T2I task, we fine-tune the model using a LoRA adapter with a rank of 32" (Sec. 4.1)

name: AsymRnR
backbones: CogVideoX-2B; CogVideoX-5B; Mochi-1; HunyuanVideo; FastVideo-Hunyuan; AnimateDiff
main_result: HunyuanVideo: VBench 0.8237 at 703.29 s, 1.30x (baseline 0.8157 at 912.98 s), fast setting, H100; CogVideoX-2B 1.17x at VBench 0.7849 (ToMe-fast 1.16x at 0.7732)
notes: Reduction is applied inside self-attention of video DiTs after the Q, K, V projections: Q and the K/V pair are reduced separately by ToMe-style bipartite soft matching with their own rates, attention runs on the shorter sequences, and only the Q sequence is restored to full length. Which feature, block and timestep is reduced is decided by thresholding a similarity map estimated in advance from arbitrary sampling (context-agnostic, so the schedule is the same for every prompt; mapped to learned-rate as an offline search). Matching results are cached for s = 5 steps. Latency on A100 (CogVideoX) or H100 (others); batch size not stated.
evidence: "We propose Asymmetric Reduction and Restoration (AsymRnR), a training-free and model-agnostic method to accelerate video DiTs." (Abstract); "Unlike previous works that focus on reducing H, we reduce Q and K&V independently" (Sec. 3.3); "it is sufficient to restore the Q sequence" (Sec. 3.3); "Fortunately, we can leverage the property that similarity patterns are context-agnostic, enabling the similarity distribution to be estimated in advance through arbitrary diffusion sampling." (Sec. 3.4)

name: SparseDiT
main_result: DiT-XL ImageNet 512x512: FID 3.13 at 235 GFLOPs, 0.685 img/s (DiT-XL 3.04 at 525 GFLOPs, 0.249 img/s), r in [0.90, 0.96], A100 batch 128
notes: Three segments: poolingformers (global average pooling of V instead of attention) in the bottom layers, sparse-dense token modules in the middle, dense transformers at the top. In each module M sparse tokens are initialized by adaptive spatial pooling of the dense tokens and refined by cross-attention to them, processed by sparse transformers, then upsampled, fused with the dense tokens and refined by a reverse cross-attention (resample + reactivate). No token scoring. The pruning rate r = 1 - M/N is held at r_min for the first T/4 steps and then changes linearly with the step (same rule for every image). Fine-tuned from pretrained DiTs (400K iterations for DiT-XL, about 6% of pretraining). No code URL found in the paper text.
evidence: "These sparse tokens can be initialized by adaptively pooling the dense tokens X." (Sec. 3.1); "Sparse token interact with full-size dense tokens via an attention layer to integrate the global information" (Sec. 3.1); "we utilize an attention layer to perform a reverse operation of the generation of sparse token to produce the restored dense tokens" (Sec. 3.1); "We exploit this by dynamically adjusting the pruning rate r across sampling steps, increasing tokens as sampling progresses." (Sec. 3.2); "Our method fine-tunes pre-trained DiT models to improve efficiency." (Sec. 3.3)

name: FlexiDiT
backbones: DiT-XL/2; T2I Transf. (PixArt-style); Emu 1.7B DiT; Video DiT 4.9B
main_result: T2I Transf. 256x256 MS COCO: FID 14.71 / CLIP 25.58 at 58% of baseline FLOPs (baseline 14.75 / 25.60 at 100%); video: up to 75% less compute without a significant VBench drop
notes: One DiT is made to accept a second, 2x larger patch size (4x fewer tokens) through new embedding / de-embedding layers (projected with the pseudo-inverse of bilinear interpolation) and patch-size embeddings. The inference scheduler runs the first T_weak denoising steps with the large patch size and the rest with the original one (fixed rule, same for every image); the weak model can also serve as the guidance signal. Class-conditioned DiT-XL/2 is fully fine-tuned; T2I and video models keep frozen weights with per-patch-size LoRAs trained by distillation (backbone frozen). Results are reported mainly in FLOPs; latency appears only as relative latency of CFG packing variants (App., Fig. 12) and a roofline analysis on H100. No code URL in the paper.
evidence: "We instead propose to use different patch sizes at different steps in the denoising process of the same image." (Sec. 3); "by leveraging bigger patch sizes only for early steps, we can reduce the overall generation time while maintaining both low and high-frequency details in the produced images" (Sec. 3); "We obtain a flexible model — coined FlexiDiT — by modifying and fine-tuning a pre-trained DiT" (Sec. 3); "we freeze the original weights and add trainable LoRAs" (Sec. 3.2)

name: RAS
main_result: SD3 1024x1024 COCO: FID 31.99 / CLIP 30.64 at 1.45 img/s with 7 steps and 25% sampling ratio (RFlow 5 steps: 39.70 / 29.84 at 1.43 img/s); up to 2.36x (SD3) and 2.51x (Lumina-Next-T2I) speed-up
notes: At each denoising step only the fast-update tokens are passed through the DiT; the other tokens reuse the noise predicted at the previous step and stay in attention as cached keys and values, so halt is the closest operation (a per-token feature cache across steps). Token score = standard deviation of the previous step's predicted noise per patch times exp(k x drop count). Top tokens by a user-set sampling ratio; the first steps are dense, the ratio is then reduced and some dense steps are inserted (hand-set rule). Throughput on one A100 80GB; batch size not stated. No code URL in the paper text.
evidence: "we introduce RAS, a training-free sampling strategy that dynamically adjusts update ratios across image regions based on model attention" (Abstract); "Only these regions are forwarded through the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) for denoising, while the remaining slow-update regions reuse the cached noise from the previous step." (Sec. 1); "features from slow-update regions are retained as reference keys and values for subsequent attention computations" (Sec. 1); "we analyze the model’s noise output and observe that the standard deviation of predicted noise effectively distinguishes different semantic regions" (Sec. 3.2); "the initial few steps (e.g., the first 4 out of 28) are executed with a full 100% sampling ratio to preserve the global image outline, after which the ratio is gradually reduced as the generation stabilizes" (Sec. 3.3)

name: SiTo
backbones: Stable Diffusion v1.5; Stable Diffusion v2 (U-Net)
main_result: SD v1.5 512x512 ImageNet (2,000 images): FID 26.31 at 1.37 s/img, 1.90x (baseline 27.64 at 2.61 s/img), RTX 4090; COCO30K FID 11.17 at 1.75x (baseline 12.32)
notes: Tokens are the latent tokens of the U-Net transformer blocks (self-attention by default). In each s x s region the token with the highest sum of cosine similarity to all tokens (plus Gaussian noise to vary the choice across steps) becomes a base token; the K non-base tokens most similar to a base token are pruned, the rest pass the layer, and pruned tokens are recovered by copying their most similar base token. Same count for every image. No calibration data. Latency on one RTX 4090; batch size not stated.
evidence: "SiTo selects the tokens that have the highest similarity to the base tokens as the pruned tokens." (Introduction); "SiTo feeds the unpruned tokens to the neural layers and recovers the pruned tokens by directly copying their most similar base tokens." (Introduction); "we propose to add Gaussian noise to the similarity of different tokens, which introduces randomness during base token selection" (Introduction); "we prune the same number of tokens for all the images in the same batch" (Pruned Token Selection); "SiTo has no training requirements and does not require any calibration data" (Abstract)

name: Fourier Token Merging
main_result: SD v1.5 (ImageNet class prompts, 2,000 images): up to 25% lower latency than the full model without loss of image quality; FID vs latency against ToMeSD only as curves (Fig. 5), RTX 4090
notes: ToMeSD with a different similarity space: each token's channel vector is transformed by a DFT, the real part is truncated to the lowest tau*d frequencies, and bipartite soft matching on these vectors decides which tokens merge; merged tokens go through attention and are unmerged for the ResNet blocks. The truncation ratio tau changes with timestep and layer depth by a hand-set interpolation; the merging ratio per block is fixed. Applied to the five transformer blocks with downsampling level at most 1. Batch size not stated.
evidence: "transforming the token into the frequency domain representation for clustering can better exert the ability of clustering based on the underlying redundancy after de-correlation" (Abstract); "The clustering component employing the same bipartite soft matching then identifies and clusters tokens based on the frequency structures." (Sec. 3.1); "Since the subsequent ResNet requires the full number of tokens, tokens are unmerged to their original length" (Sec. 3.1); "can be applied to pretrained diffusion models without retraining" (Sec. 3.1); "We experiment with various merging ratios—i.e., different degrees of token count reduction per transformer block" (Sec. 5.1)

notes: Pattern Recognition 164, 111479. Full text is behind the Elsevier paywall, with no OA or arXiv version; Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and the Elsevier abstract API return no abstract. Only the title is known (token-aware and step-aware acceleration of Stable Diffusion), so all axes are unknown.

name: DeSparsify
backbones: DeiT-S; DeiT-T; T2T-ViT-19 (with ATS, AdaViT, A-ViT)
main_result: DeiT-S + ATS (ImageNet, 1,000 images): single-image attack raises GFLOPs from 3.09 to 4.20 (non-sparsified 4.6) at accuracy 88.2% (clean 88.5%); A-ViT reaches 4.6 GFLOPs, no token dropped
notes: Analysis (attack) paper, not a reduction method. Adversarial perturbations with a loss on each mechanism's keep decision make the input-adaptive token sparsification of ATS, AdaViT and A-ViT keep almost all tokens while the class prediction stays; the single-image attack recovers 74%, 44% and 100% of the GFLOPs that ATS, AdaViT and A-ViT save on DeiT-S, and on ATS raises GPU memory by 37% and energy by 72% (RTX 3090). A per-block upper bound on kept tokens is proposed as a defense (ATS: 4.2 to 3.17 GFLOPs under attack).
evidence: "we present DeSparsify, an attack targeting the availability of vision transformers that use token sparsification mechanisms" (Abstract); "The single-image attack variant, in which a perturbation is tailored to each image, results in the greatest performance degradation, increasing the GFLOPS values by 74%, 44%, and 100% for the ATS, AdaViT, and A-ViT, respectively." (Sec. 5.2); "an upper bound can be set to the number of tokens used in each transformer block" (Sec. 6)

name: SlowFormer
backbones: ViT-Ti; ViT-S; ViT-B (with A-ViT, ATS, AdaViT)
main_result: A-ViT ViT-S ImageNet: a universal 64x64 patch (8% of the image) raises GFLOPs from 3.7 to 4.6 (Attack Success 99%, top-1 78.8% to 2.3%); ATS ViT-S 3.1 to 4.0 GFLOPs (60%); AdaViT ViT-S 2.25 to 3.2 (40%)
notes: Analysis (attack) paper, not a reduction method. One universal adversarial patch, optimized on the ImageNet train set, pushes input-adaptive token reduction (A-ViT, ATS, AdaViT) back toward full compute on any image; on A-ViT it undoes 99 to 100% of the FLOPs savings, and adversarial training reduces part of the effect. Only FLOPs are reported, as a proxy for energy.
evidence: "We show that such models can be vulnerable to a universal adversarial patch attack, where the attacker optimizes for a patch that when pasted on any image, can increase the compute and power consumption of the model." (Abstract); "Our attack has an Attack Success of 60% on ATS and 40% on AdaViT with ViT-Small." (Sec. 5.1); "we do not experiment with real hardware to measure the power consumption" (Sec. 1)

backbones: ViT-Ti/S/B; DeiT-S; EViT-S; DynamicViT-S; EViT Fuse-S; ToMe-S; TokenLearner-S; STViT-Swin-Ti; CaiT-S and about 35 other efficient models
main_result: ImageNet-1k top-1 with the same IN-21k pretraining and 224px fine-tuning: ViT-S 82.54, EViT-S 82.29, ToMe-S (r = 8) 82.11, DynamicViT-S 81.09, TokenLearner-8-75-S 80.69; throughput and memory only in Pareto plots (A100)
notes: Benchmark paper, not a reduction method. More than 45 efficient ViTs, including token-sequence methods (EViT, DynamicViT, ToMe, TokenLearner, STViT, CaiT), are trained with one DeiT III pipeline and compared on accuracy, throughput at optimal batch size, training time and memory; plain ViT stays Pareto optimal for speed, while ToMe and TokenLearner are among the Pareto-optimal models for inference speed and training memory (TokenLearner-8-50-S fastest to fine-tune at 77.35%). The token reduction modules are used during training, not as plug-ins.
evidence: "we perform a large-scale benchmark of more than 45 models for image classification, evaluating key efficiency aspects, including accuracy, speed, and memory usage" (Abstract); "Surprisingly, despite claims of other models being more efficient, ViT remains Pareto optimal across multiple metrics." (Abstract); "While some of these methods can directly be applied to trained models, performance improves when implementing them during training [5], which we do." (Sec. 3.3); "Generally, ViT is still a solid choice for speed, with some Token Sequence models trading off accuracy for speed." (Sec. 5.3)
